analysis.one_liner: Directs EPA to tighten drinking water and indoor-air safety limits for the industrial solvent trichloroethylene.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to tighten trichloroethylene safety standards cleared the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee without amendment in September 2008 but was never brought to a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Trichloroethylene (TCE) is a metal degreaser and solvent ingredient whose waste is widespread in soil and water; the bill's findings cite more than 1,000 contaminated waste sites, links to kidney cancer and leukemia, and risks to pregnant women, infants, and children. The bill would have required the EPA to issue a health advisory for TCE in drinking water within 180 days that fully protects those susceptible groups, and to set a stricter national drinking water limit. It also would have required water utilities to tell customers about TCE in their water, and directed EPA to set a protective limit for TCE vapors that seep from contaminated groundwater into indoor air and to apply it at Superfund and other cleanup sites.
analysis.who_benefits: People who drink from public water supplies with trichloroethylene contamination, and people living above contaminated groundwater or soil where TCE vapors can seep into homes and buildings — the bill specifically requires protections for pregnant women, infants, and children, who are most vulnerable. The EPA's own findings cited in the bill note the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry estimated that between 9 and 34 percent of drinking water supply sources have some TCE contamination.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families near TCE-contaminated water and sites

how_it_helps.text: Requires EPA, within 180 days, to publish a trichloroethylene health advisory that fully protects pregnant women, infants, and children with an adequate margin of safety, accounting for body weight, exposure patterns, and all routes of exposure.

Requires a new national drinking water regulation for trichloroethylene, with the maximum contaminant level set as close to the health goal as feasible, replacing the existing 5 micrograms per liter limit that the bill's findings note EPA's own 2001 assessment suggested lowering to 1 microgram per liter.
Requires water utilities' annual consumer confidence reports to disclose trichloroethylene in drinking water and its specific risks to pregnant women, infants, and children.

Requires EPA to set a trichloroethylene vapor reference concentration protective of susceptible populations and apply it to cleanup investigations under Superfund and the Safe Drinking Water Act, addressing the indoor-air pathway ('vapor intrusion') from contaminated groundwater and soil.

analysis.who_pays: Water systems and their ratepayers, who would bear monitoring and treatment costs to meet a stricter limit; and industries, current or former site owners, and government cleanup programs responsible for TCE contamination, who would face higher remediation costs as EPA applies a stricter vapor-intrusion standard at Superfund and other sites.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs would fall on public water systems: the bill requires revised monitoring for all systems, state review of monitoring waivers near contamination sites, and a stricter national drinking water standard, and water systems generally recover those costs from ratepayers.

By requiring EPA to apply a stricter trichloroethylene vapor reference concentration to Superfund and other hazardous-waste investigations, the bill would raise cleanup costs at contaminated sites, and the bill's findings acknowledge more than 1,000 trichloroethylene waste sites nationwide.

The bill sets hard statutory deadlines (180 days for a health advisory, 18 months for a final drinking water regulation) and requires the standard to be as close to the maximum contaminant level goal as feasible, which critics could argue forces EPA to set standards on an accelerated timetable with significant cost implications.
The committee reported the bill with minority views filed, indicating that Senate Environment and Public Works Republicans registered formal objections to the bill as reported.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are substantial and well-documented: TCE is one of the most common groundwater contaminants in the country, the National Academy of Sciences had strengthened the evidence tying it to kidney cancer and leukemia, and the bill required protections specifically for pregnant women, infants, and children on a firm deadline. The costs are real but ordinary for environmental regulation: water systems would face monitoring and treatment expenses likely passed to ratepayers, and stricter cleanup standards would raise remediation costs at contaminated sites. On balance, the bill asked the parties responsible for a widespread solvent to internalize its costs, and gave the EPA deadlines rather than discretion. The main design criticism is that hard statutory deadlines can force EPA to set standards on a faster clock than careful science allows.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate environment committee approved it and put it on the Senate's calendar of business, but Senate leadership never brought it up for a vote before the two-year Congress ran out.

narrative.text: Senator Hillary Clinton introduced the bill on August 1, 2007, joined by eight senators including Republican Elizabeth Dole, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.
On July 31, 2008, the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee ordered the bill reported favorably without amendment.
The committee formally reported the bill on September 24, 2008, with a written report and minority views filed by committee members who disagreed.
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on September 24, 2008, but no floor vote ever occurred before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Parties facing potential cleanup liability for trichloroethylene contamination avoided a stricter federal cleanup standard, and water systems avoided new monitoring and treatment costs; communities near contaminated sites got no new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: TCE users, liable site owners, water systems

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Democrat (Clinton) and a Republican (Dole) with 8 total original sponsors, and cleared committee without amendment; committee Republicans filed minority views, and no floor vote ever occurred to reveal a party split.

industries.industry: TCE users and contaminated-site owners (metal degreasing, adhesives, paint removers)
industries.note: The bill would apply a stricter trichloroethylene vapor reference concentration to Superfund and other cleanup actions, raising remediation liability at sites where past use or disposal contaminated soil and groundwater. The bill's findings count more than 1,000 such waste sites.

Water systems would face revised monitoring requirements, state review of monitoring waivers near contamination sites, and potentially costly treatment to meet a stricter drinking water standard, with costs typically recovered through water rates.
Stricter health advisories, monitoring, and mandated application of a tighter vapor reference concentration to Superfund investigations would generate additional testing and cleanup work.
A stricter drinking water standard and vapor-intrusion limits would increase the regulatory and liability exposure tied to trichloroethylene, a widely used chlorinated solvent.
